items.title: Ashanti Regional Minister cautions students against indiscipline and teachers’ attacks
items.description: Dr Frank Amoakohene, Ashanti Regional Minister, has cautioned students against acts of vandalism and attacks on teachers in their various campuses. He said the rising spate of assaults on teachers and destruction of school properties by some students as reported in the media, was worrying and there was the need for students to put a stop to it, since such behavior could derail academic work and compromise educational environment. Dr Amoakohene made the call, when he addressed students of Kumasi Academy (KUMACA) at the launch of the school’s 70th anniversary logo and cloth at the school auditorium in Kumasi. The anniversary will be held under the theme: “Shaping character, cultivating minds, and nurturing souls.” The official launch marks the formal commencement of a year-long calendar of milestone activities leading up to the grand anniversary durbar. Activities lined up include a health walk, exhibition, fun-filled games, a speech and prize-giving day, entertainment, and thanksgiving services. The global alumni associations including branches in the United States and the United Kingdom are also mobilising resources to fund critical infrastructure development on campus. They include the expansion of the school’s newly completed dormitory blocks and upgrading dining hall facilities. Dr Amoakohene stated that Kumasi Academy had long been recognised for discipline and urged students not to allow the hard-earned reputation of the school to be undermined by indiscipline. He appealed to the students to continue observing the strict standards of discipline instilled by the Baptist missionaries. Referencing a recent incident at Obuasi Secondary Technical School, where the headmaster was attacked and school property vandalised, he described the conduct as unacceptable and called for no repetition in any institution. He explained that teacher discipline did not necessarily reflect hatred, but rather, a structured approach to preparing students to become responsible and productive citizens. Mr Samuel Gato, Headmaster of Kumasi Academy, said the school had produced distinguished individuals and prominent personalities since 1957, making the commemoration of 70 years a momentous milestone deserving of celebration. He said it was a shared responsibility among contemporary leaders and alumni to organise and mark the occasion in honour of the school’s past, and therefore encouraged students, alumni, and relevant stakeholders to collaborate and make sacrifices towards the successful celebration slated for next year, 2027. The event was graced by Nana Boakye Yam Ababio II (Nkwantakesehene); Mr Amo Kamel, the MCE for Asokwa; Mr Ben Abdullah Alhassan, the MCE for Asokore-Mampong; heads of institutions; together with members of the clergy, staff, and students.

items.title: IMF urges Ghana to sustain quarterly electricity tariff adjustments‎
items.description: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has urged Ghana to sustain quarterly electricity tariff adjustments to reduce fiscal risks in the energy sector. ‎The sector shortfall declined to US$1.4 billion in 2025 from US$1.6 billion in 2024, but remained a significant pressure on public finances.‎ ‎The IMF said in its 2026 Article IV Consultation and Sixth Review under the Extended Credit Facility (ECF) that sustained reforms were needed to consolidate the gains and improve the sector’s financial sustainability.‎ ‎“Despite progress, challenges remain in transforming the sector from a source of fiscal risks to a driver of inclusive growth,” the IMF said.‎ ‎The Fund attributed the improvement to tariff adjustments, enhanced revenue collection by the Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG), reduced use of liquid fuels in power generation, cedi appreciation and increased payments to energy suppliers through the Cash Waterfall Mechanism.‎ ‎It said the sector’s shortfall was projected at about US$1.1 billion in 2026, driven largely by high collection and distribution losses and costly generation contracts.‎ ‎The report noted that the Public Utilities Regulatory Commission (PURC) reduced electricity tariffs by 4.81 per cent in April 2026 before increasing them by 3.49 per cent in July 2026 under the quarterly tariff adjustment mechanism.‎ ‎The IMF said maintaining the tariff adjustment framework was critical to narrowing the energy sector financing gap, improving cost recovery and ensuring the sector’s ability to meet obligations to independent power producers (IPPs) and fuel suppliers.‎ ‎It also acknowledged government’s efforts to reduce legacy debts in the sector.‎ ‎Net payables owed to IPPs and fuel suppliers declined to US$1.7 billion by March 2026 from US$2.1 billion at the end of 2024, following debt renegotiations and payments made through government interventions.‎ ‎The Fund said the government secured savings through the renegotiation of power purchase agreements and legacy debt obligations, while making substantial payments to energy suppliers, including those linked to the Sankofa gas project.‎ ‎It recommended strict adherence to quarterly tariff reviews, regular publication of audit reports on ECG’s revenue collection accounts and full implementation of the Cash Waterfall Mechanism.‎ ‎The report also identified increased private-sector participation in electricity distribution as a key reform.‎ ‎It said a transaction adviser had been appointed to facilitate the procurement of concessionaires, with the concessions expected to be awarded by June 2027.‎ ‎The IMF said private-sector participation was expected to reduce technical and commercial losses, improve revenue mobilisation and strengthen operational efficiency within the power distribution system.‎ ‎It stressed that achieving a financially sustainable energy sector would require continued policy discipline and reforms beyond the current IMF-supported programme.‎ ‎The Fund said a more efficient and financially sound energy sector was necessary to support economic growth, attract investment and reduce pressure on public finances.‎

items.title: Woman ‘tortured’ for taking possession of grabbed land in Sahiwal
items.description: SAHIWAL: A woman, who had taken possession of her inherited land after being illegally occupied for around 30 years, was allegedly abducted, tortured and humiliated by 12 armed attackers, including three women, at Chak 93/9-L. The victim, Mardan Bibi, got possession of her land she had inherited under Ghori Pal Scheme, with the help of Pera Force, police, revenue department and the district administration, following 30 years of illegal occupation. As per the First Information Report (FIR), registered under sections 50, 148, 149, 447, 511, 365, and 354 of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC) on the complaint of her son, Nomir Abbas, the attackers, armed with pistols and rifles, kidnapped Mardan Bibi, subjected her to torture, and fled on the arrival of a team of Yousafwala police, which came to rescue her. As per police sources, the land inherited by the victim had been illegally occupied by one Khudayar Baloch and others for nearly three decades. After repeated appeals by Mardan Bibi, Sahiwal Commissioner Asif Tufail ordered the revenue department, Punjab Enforcement and Regulatory Authority (Pera) Force, and district administration officials to restore possession of the land to the legal owner, Mardan Bibi. Accordingly, in an operation led by Assistant Commissioner Nouman Qasir, the land was retrieved from illegal occupants and its possession was given to the complainant. However, as soon as the officials team left the village, Khudayar Baloch, Ali, Sarfraz, Yaseen Baloch, Gulaan Bibi, Nooran, Sheenan, Allah Maafi, and their four unidentified accomplices returned with arms. The FIR says that the suspects dragged the victim by her hair, and forcibly took her away on a motorcycle, after covering her face with a piece of cloth. When her cousin Akram tried to intervene, he was injured by the suspects. However, the police, on being informed of the attack on the 15 helpline, arrived at the scene, rescued the woman and arrested six of the suspects, while others managed to escape. The police say raids are underway to apprehend the fleeing suspects. Published in Dawn, August 11th, 2026

items.title: Christians urged to balance faith with healthcare
items.description: Dr Angel Abena Tiwaa, a Medical Officer, has urged Christians to combine faith in divine healing with healthy lifestyles and professional medical care. She advised Christians not to rely solely on prayer when ill but to seek appropriate medical attention, follow professional advice and adopt healthy habits. Dr Tiwaa gave the advice on Sunday during a “Health Sunday” service organised by Resurrection Power and Living Bread Ministries International, Dansoman–My Father’s House, on the theme: “Stewarding the Family’s Health.” She said Christians could pursue health through three complementary avenues: faith in divine healing, healthy living and professional healthcare. Dr Tiwaa said while Christians could trust God for supernatural healing, they should also recognise when medical attention was necessary and adhere to medical advice. She cited James 5:14-15 and Isaiah 53:5 as biblical references supporting Christian belief in divine healing. The Medical Officer, however, cautioned against treating divine health as automatic, saying believers needed to develop their faith and grow spiritually. She encouraged Christians to strengthen their spiritual lives through prayer, Bible reading, Bible study and meditation, rather than waiting until illness or crisis before developing their faith. Referring to 1 Peter 2:2-3, John 1:12, Romans 8:14 and Hebrews 5:14, she said salvation was the beginning of the Christian journey and believers needed to mature spiritually and learn to be led by the Spirit of God. Dr Tiwaa said diet, stress and sleep could significantly affect physical and mental health and should therefore be given appropriate attention. She encouraged families to eat healthy foods, exercise regularly, get adequate sleep and manage stress. Quoting Proverbs 17:22, Dr Tiwaa said: “A cheerful heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones.” She acknowledged that medicine had limitations and continued to evolve but said that was not a reason to reject professional healthcare. Dr Tiwaa said patients had a responsibility to follow medical advice and seek clarification from healthcare professionals about their conditions, treatment and preventive measures. “If you have been given a gift and you cherish the giver, you take care of it well,” she said, urging parents to protect, nurture and prepare their children for the future. Dr Tiwaa said health stewardship extended beyond hospital visits and required individuals and families to take deliberate steps to protect their health. She urged families to acquire reliable health information and use platforms such as social media for health education while being cautious about the accuracy of information obtained online. Dr Tiwaa also encouraged parents to promote physical activity, including walking, make healthier food choices and reduce consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages. She advised parents to learn about children’s developmental milestones and take an active interest in their physical and developmental well-being.

items.title: Informal peace structures critical to conflict prevention – Peace Council
items.description: The National Peace Council (NPC) has underscored the importance of informal peace structures in providing early warning information to prevent conflicts from escalating into violence. The Reverend Dr Emmanuel Badu Amoah, Ashanti Regional Executive Secretary of the NPC, said community-based actors, including religious leaders, traditional authorities, local watchdog committees and other influential individuals, often had access to vital information on emerging tensions long before such issues came to the attention of formal security and governance institutions. He was speaking at a training programme for peace ambassadors drawn from 12 constituencies in the Ashanti Region. Rev Dr Badu Amoah said although Ghana had established formal peace and security structures, informal networks within communities remained a critical source of information for identifying potential conflicts and facilitating timely interventions. “Somebody in the community may tell you that tomorrow there is going to be a confrontation between the two groups. That is an informal peace infrastructure, and that information is valuable,” he said. He explained that during election periods, for example, community members who observed activities such as the destruction or removal of campaign posters, or other developments likely to heighten tensions, could alert the appropriate authorities for prompt action. Rev Dr Badu Amoah said the challenge was to strengthen coordination between informal peace structures and the formal peace architecture to ensure that information gathered at the community level was properly assessed and acted upon before conflicts escalated. He said the training programme was designed to equip participants with the knowledge and skills needed to identify early warning signs, understand conflict issues, and support intervention efforts. Participants included religious leaders, representatives of community watchdog committees and personnel from the Ghana Police Service, Ghana Immigration Service and Ghana National Fire Service. Rev Dr Badu Amoah said religious leaders were particularly important to the initiative because of their influence within communities and their ability to promote peaceful coexistence and mediate disputes. He said the Council sought to build a network of peace ambassadors who would make peacebuilding an intentional part of their responsibilities and serve as representatives of the NPC in their respective communities. According to him, the ambassadors would help address issues such as drug abuse, family disputes, communal tensions, and other emerging conflicts, while promoting the values of unity, tolerance and peaceful coexistence. “Our purpose is that if something is happening that can escalate into violence, we will not allow it to happen. We want to start the process of resolving the issue and dealing with it before we get to violence,” he said. Rev Dr Badu Amoah said strengthening community-level early warning systems was essential to protecting Ghana’s peace and stability and preventing conditions that could create opportunities for violent extremism and terrorism. He said the NPC would continue to engage religious and community groups to expand the network and ensure that relevant information from communities reached the appropriate institutions in a timely manner.

items.title: Globe Tower – A new landmark rises in Cantonments City
items.description: A new landmark is taking shape on the Accra skyline, and it is now leasing. Globe Tower, the latest Grade A development within Cantonments City, brings premium office space and a signature third-floor restaurant to one of the capital’s most prestigious enclaves, with a limited number of floors now available to forward-looking organizations. Scheduled for completion in the second quarter of 2027, the tower marks the next chapter in a district that has redefined how Accra Works, Lives, and Unwinds. With completion approaching in 2027, only a limited number of floors remain at the very center of Accra’s most dynamic enclave. To explore the space and discuss terms, contact Goldkey Properties on 055 588 7777 or 055 588 7799, or visit www.goldkeyghana.com to arrange a private viewing. Designed by the acclaimed Magna 5 Group, Globe Tower rises from a columned ground floor through thirteen upper storeys as a contemporary institutional landmark. Its strong rectilinear form and consistent grid facade project stability, professionalism, and a global corporate presence. At its heart, a dramatic central atrium frames a suspended globe, the building’s striking visual centerpiece and a fitting symbol for organizations with national reach and global ambition. Landscaped terraces soften the tower’s scale, while the open base invites pedestrian flow and a welcoming sense of accessibility. Crafted in durable, high-quality materials with generous glazing, the building balances monumentality with light-filled, human-scaled interiors. The setting is as compelling as the architecture. Cantonments City is Accra’s most sought-after address, and Globe Tower sits within minutes of the seat of government at Jubilee House, the Police Headquarters, the United Nations offices, and the American, Korean and Chinese embassies. Accra International Airport and the Central Business District are both within easy reach, the kind of connectivity that matters to top multinationals, local corporates and institutions deciding where to headquarter. Crucially, Globe Tower is not a standalone building but part of Cantonments City, Ghana’s first branded mixed-use enclave and a fully integrated live-work-unwind environment. The district is home to Grade A buildings, supports more than 2,000 people at work each day, and provides over 1,200 secure parking bays, along with continuous power, water, security, ambulance services, and professional property management. It also includes dining, leisure and a landscaped green park lie within the enclave, and its award-winning, environmentally conscious design helps keep both operating costs and carbon in check. For tenants, it is an address that signals permanence and prestige to clients, partners and talent alike. Globe Tower is developed by Goldkey Properties, a fully Ghanaian-owned developer established in 1997 and a member of the CH Group. Over nearly three decades, Goldkey has delivered more than 300,000 square meters of residential and commercial space and built eight Grade A buildings across Cantonments City, earning the confidence of blue-chip occupiers including EY, PwC, Huawei and Vivo Energy, and collecting international, continental and national honors over the years. As part of the CH Group, whose interests span energy, financial services and real estate, Goldkey pairs institutional-grade delivery with a depth of resources and services few developers can match. With completion approaching in 2027, only a limited number of floors remain at the very center of Accra’s most dynamic enclave. To explore the space and discuss terms, contact Goldkey Properties on 055 588 7777 or 055 588 7799, or visit www.goldkeyghana.com to arrange a private viewing.

items.title: Corporate Ghana, international community donate to government June 29 flood victims
items.description: The Office of the President has received cash contributions, medical supplies, food, and essential humanitarian goods from various corporate organisations and institutions to support victims of the devastating 29 June 2026 flood disaster. A statement issued by the Presidency said the torrential rains and subsequent flooding severely impacted several parts of the country, particularly the capital, Accra. It said a wave of corporate philanthropists have poured into the Presidency to support ongoing post-flood mitigation and relief efforts by the Government. It said senior government officials, including Nana Oye Bampoe Addo, Deputy Chief of Staff at the Presidency in-charge of Finance and Administration; Madam Marietta Agyeiwaa Brew, the Legal Advisor to the President, and Mrs Joyce Bawa Mogtari, Presidential Adviser and Special Aide to the President, received the items on behalf of the state. The statement said cash contributions were SoftCare FM Manufacturing Company Limited GH₵ 200,000.00 and Ghana Institute of Surveyors GH₵ 50,000.00. It said major corporate and organisational donors included Ghana Association of Chinese Societies and Companies: 1,112 bags of rice (2.5kg), 4,000 bags of sachet water, 500 cartons of sunflower oil, 490 cartons of Frytol oil, 490 cartons of canned mackerel and 646 cartons of Kivo gari. Others are 501 cartons of spaghetti, 295 cartons of sardines, 235 cartons of biscuits, 208 cartons of tomato paste, 70 boxes of chocolate cake, 50 cartons of shito and other assorted provisions. The rest were 2,000 painless malaria rapid test kits, 800 cartons of HPV test kits, 1 box of Coartem (anti-malaria medication), 80 gallons of hand sanitiser, 79 bottles of disinfectant alcohol, 3,000 sleeping mats, 400 school bags, 3,200 T-shirts, 3,100 plastic buckets, 3,000 plastic basins, and 5 stainless steel 2,000-litre water tanks. Furthermore, three chest freezers, 32 electric cookers, 34 electric fans, 200 bundles of shovels, 120 cartons of mosquito coils, and Temporary shelter/bedding materials. and Temporary shelter/bedding materials. The statement said Scancom Plc (MTN Ghana), supported by Multimedia Company Limited’s Flood Relief Campaign on radio and television provided 1,400 student mattresses, 1,192 blankets, 998 relief boxes packed with essential food items, blankets, mosquito repellents, nets, and detergents. It said Sentuo Group Limited donated 4,000 bags of rice (25kg), 600 bags of sugar (50kg) and 387 boxes of granular maize. The statement said Ecobank Ghana also donated 10 boxes of paracetamol, 10 boxes of hydrolyte, four boxes of Gastrone suspension, along with Ascovit-Cee, Epanol, Permonyl, Nencofer syrup/capsules, dewormers, rubbing alcohol, and antimalarials, 1,000 bags of sachet water, 195 mattresses, 250 blankets and bales of used clothing for men, women, and children. It said Softcare FM Manufacturing Company Limited provided 100 bags of KleenSoft washing powder & 100 boxes of KleenSoft soap, 100 boxes of sanitary pads and 50 boxes of baby diapers. The statement noted that B5 Plus Limited donated 70 bags of rice (50kg), 100 bags of maize (50kg), 50 cartons of Cerelac baby food, 75 jerrycans of cooking oil, 50 cartons of sardines and bottled water, 200 blankets, 200 jerrycans (2L), 150 mosquito nets, 100 pairs of Wellington boots and 100 raincoats. It said Eezzy Group also donated 178 bags of rice (50kg), 842 bags of rice (2.5kg), 120 cartons of spaghetti, 72 boxes of canned beef, 46 cartons of sardines, 22 cartons of tomato paste and 82 cartons of cooking oil (various sizes), seasoning powders, and baking supplies. The statement said Tobinco Group donated 100 boxes of Omal antiseptic, 5,000 gallons of Omal liquid soap, and 400 gallons of Omazone bleach whiles Kam Trading & Farms Limited donated 445 bags of 25kg rice.

items.title: Tourism Minister outlines government’s strategic decision to revamp Du Bois Centre
items.description: Abla Dzifa Gomashie, the Minister of Tourism, Culture and Creative Arts, says the Government’s decision to review and sign an agreement with the Du Bois Foundation in the United States to hand over the W.E.B. Du Bois Centre will strengthen cultural diplomacy. The Minister who disclosed this when she took her turn at the Government’s said it would also preserve historical authenticity and enhance global visibility. She reiterated that it was anticipated that the partnership would bring technical expertise, international funding, and stronger archival and research capacity, ensuring that the vision and intellectual heritage of W.E.B. Du Bois were professionally managed and globally connected. She noted that it would also deepen ties between Ghana and the African diaspora, positioning the Centre as a vibrant hub for Pan-African scholarship, tourism, and cultural exchange while reinforcing Ghana’s leadership in honoring shared Black history. She said they hoped to upgrade the Du Bois Centre to the level of the Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park. Touching on Improvement of the Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park, the Minister said upon assumption of office, we have subjected the Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park (KNMP) to a deliberate governance and institutional restructuring. She noted that a Governing Board was constituted in October 2025 for the first time for the Park and supported by a clarified organogram and reporting structure. “The Park’s redesigned website has been active since June 2025 and now includes a virtual tour,” Madam Gomashie said. “Social media engagement has increased significantly, with Facebook followers growing from 475 to over 14,200 within eight months.” She said refresh branding and improved signage had enhanced visibility; adding that visitor experience had improved through redesigning the facility, free Wi-Fi, and installation of 25 marble benches. She said there had been major infrastructure upgrades including lighting rewiring, restoration of the musical fountain, landscaping improvements, repainting of the Park, and reinforcement of concrete drain covers with metal grids. “Energy costs an average of GHS100,000 monthly. An energy audit has been completed, transformer upgrades undertaken, and a solar transition is underway, expected to be completed before end-March.” She said plans were advanced to operationalise the Dr Kwame Nkrumah Presidential Library, in collaboration with the Ghana Library Authority; saying, “opening is expected during the 2026 Nkrumah Fest”.

items.title: Security agencies urged to act against religious hate speech‎
items.description: Adib Saani, Executive Director of the Jatikay Centre for Human Security and Peace Building, has urged security agencies to act firmly against religious hate and extremist speech to safeguard Ghana’s religious harmony.‎ ‎He said inflammatory religious statements could heighten tensions, provoke retaliation and undermine peaceful relations between religious communities.‎ ‎Mr Saani made the call in an interview with the Ghana News Agency (GNA) following the police’s recent invitation of an Imam to assist with investigations into allegedly religiously intolerant comments he made.‎ ‎He said the police action was necessary because of the potential of such comments to inflame religious passions.‎ ‎“I do think the invitation should have even come earlier,” he said.‎ ‎Mr Saani described the comments attributed to the Imam as dangerous and capable of evoking passions, noting that religious matters were highly sensitive and that pronouncements by religious leaders could significantly influence their followers.‎ ‎He said statements perceived as attacks on religious beliefs could trigger retaliation and counter-retaliation, potentially escalating into wider communal tensions.‎ ‎Mr Saani cited experiences from Nigeria, including the case of Mohammed Yusuf, founder of Boko Haram, to underscore the potential consequences of failing to address inflammatory religious rhetoric early.‎ ‎He urged the authorities to investigate the matter thoroughly and, where offences were established, apply the law to serve as a deterrent to others who might resort to hate or extremist speech.‎ ‎Mr Saani said religious leaders commanded significant influence and that their pronouncements were sometimes regarded by followers as authoritative, making responsible communication particularly important.‎ ‎He cautioned that inflammatory statements could be interpreted by some individuals as justification for violence and thereby create tensions between religious communities.‎ ‎Mr Saani noted that an apology reportedly issued by the Imam did not adequately address the concerns, particularly where religious teachings were invoked to justify violent responses to alleged insults against religious figures.‎ ‎He said freedom of expression should be exercised responsibly, particularly on religious matters, and stressed the need to distinguish legitimate criticism from speech that amounted to incitement, hate, intimidation or harassment.‎ ‎Mr Saani acknowledged that some individuals had allegedly made repeated provocative comments against Muslims, saying such conduct should also be examined within the broader discussion on religious tolerance and responsible speech.‎ ‎“There is a thin line between tolerance and free speech,” he said, adding that people were entitled to express their views but must remain mindful of the emotional sensitivities of others.‎ ‎Mr Saani said Ghana had largely maintained peaceful relations between Muslims and Christians despite occasional challenges and cautioned against actions that could undermine the country’s religious harmony.‎ ‎He called on religious leaders and their followers to promote tolerance and peaceful coexistence, stressing that the Prophet Muhammad had not instructed Muslims to kill people who insulted him.‎ ‎Mr Saani said his own experience, including being raised by a Muslim father who sent him to Christian mission schools, demonstrated the longstanding cooperation between the two faiths.‎ ‎He urged Ghanaians to protect that harmony as a foundation for national peace and development.‎

items.title: Gulf shipping traffic via Strait of Hormuz falls to six vessels
items.description: By Mohi Narayan NEW DELHI, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell to six on Monday, compared with a 10-day average of about 11 vessels, shipping data showed, amid fading hopes of a peace deal between the U.S. and Iran. Four commodity vessels, including two empty oil product tankers, entered the waterway, data from Kpler showed on Tuesday as of 0420 GMT. Two vessels — a small tanker laden with liquefied petroleum gas and another carrying residual fuels — exited the Strait, the data showed.

items.title: Ghana’s Ambassador to Saudi Arabia mourns Deputy Ambassador Sanni Jajah
items.description: Ghana’s Ambassador to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, Alhaji Said Sinare, has expressed profound sorrow over the death of his Deputy Ambassador, Sanni Jajah, describing him as a brother, confidant, and trusted colleague. Jajah passed away last Saturday, leaving behind a legacy of dedicated public service and diplomatic excellence. In a statement issued on Monday, Ambassador Sinare said the late deputy was more than a colleague with whom he shared diplomatic responsibilities. He described him as a dependable companion whose wisdom, counsel, and commitment greatly strengthened the work of Ghana’s Embassy in Saudi Arabia. “It has taken me several painful hours to summon the courage, composure, and strength to come to terms with the sudden and devastating demise of my beloved deputy and brother,” he said. Ambassador Sinare said Jajah was a man of exceptional character, intellectual depth, professional discipline, humility, and integrity, who served Ghana with unwavering loyalty and dedication. “His counsel was invaluable, his commitment unquestionable, and his devotion to duty evident even in the most demanding circumstances,” he said. “Mr. Jajah approached his responsibilities with maturity, discretion, wisdom, and courage, making significant contributions to Ghana’s diplomatic representation in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.” Beyond his official duties, Ambassador Sinare described the late diplomat as a warm, compassionate, and humane individual whose kindness and brotherliness touched the lives of many. “For me personally, this loss is immeasurable. I have lost a deputy, but more painfully, I have lost a brother. I have lost a trusted confidant, a valued colleague, and a man with whom I shared the burdens, responsibilities, challenges, and aspirations of representing Ghana in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” he added. The ambassador said the loss extended beyond personal grief, describing Jajah’s passing as a significant setback for the Embassy of Ghana in Riyadh, the diplomatic community, and the nation as a whole. “The Embassy has lost a distinguished officer. The diplomatic community has lost a respected colleague. Ghana has lost a committed servant of the Republic,” he stated. Ambassador Sinare extended his condolences to the bereaved family, relatives, friends, colleagues, and associates. He urged them to remember Jajah for the dignity with which he lived, the integrity with which he served, and the lasting contributions he made to the institutions and people entrusted to his care. He also prayed for Allah’s mercy upon the deceased, asking that his shortcomings be forgiven, his good deeds accepted, and that he be granted Jannatul Firdaus, the highest level of Paradise in Islam. Meanwhile, Mr. Yussif Jajah, the Deputy Minister of Tourism, Culture and Creative Arts and Member of Parliament for Ayawaso North, said in a brief statement that details of the funeral and final funeral arrangements for his nephew would be announced by the family in due course. He appealed to the public to keep the family in their thoughts and prayers during this difficult period. President John Dramani Mahama appointed Sanni Jajah as Deputy Ambassador to Saudi Arabia on September 11, 2025.

items.title: GMA facilitates repatriation of 12 stranded seafarers
items.description: The Ghana Maritime Authority (GMA) has facilitated the repatriation of 12 stranded seafarers aboard the MV Rahaf Moon through a coordinated humanitarian and regulatory intervention. An official release copied to Ghana News Agency, Monday, said the vessel, registered under the flag of St. Kitts & Nevis, was identified in Ghanaian waters on 20 January, 2026. This was done after support from its owner, ATSE Global Shipping Company Limited, ceased, leaving the crew in difficult conditions. “The crew, made up of nine Indians, two Azerbaijanis, and one Turkish national, faced prolonged hardship, including restricted access to food and fresh water, with unpaid wages exceeding US$150,000. “In response, the GMA mobilised a network of stakeholders, including the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority (GPHA), International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF), Point 3 Logistics, Boti Crew to safeguard the welfare of the seafarers and ensure compliance with international maritime obligations,” it said. Other collaborators included the vessel’s Protection and Indemnity Club, legal representatives, the Indian High Commission, and the Turkish Embassy in Ghana. GMA said emergency assistance – including food, water, fuel, and other essential supplies – was provided, while arrangements were made to maintain the safety and operational integrity of the vessel. “The intervention also led to the recovery of four months of outstanding wages for the crew before their safe repatriation to their home countries on 23 July, 2026. “Under international maritime law, seafarers’ wage claims remain protected and will continue to receive priority during the legal settlement of claims against the vessel,” the release added. “The MV Rahaf Moon, currently under the custody of the GPHA, is undergoing legal processes towards a judicial sale, with the remaining wage claims to be addressed through those proceedings.” The GMA management said it directed the deployment of a qualified Ghanaian skeletal crew to maintain security and essential onboard operations following the departure of the crew. “The Authority is also establishing a legal framework to manage proceeds from any future judicial sale of the vessel, including the settlement of approved expenses and maintenance-related claims,” it said. It reaffirmed its commitment to seafarer welfare, effective stakeholder collaboration, and adherence to international maritime standards.

items.title: Peace Council sensitises Binaba residents on online violent extremist narratives
items.description: The National Peace Council (NPC) has sensitised residents of Binaba in the Bawku West District, on the dangers of online violent extremist narratives, hate speech and fraudulent job offers used to lure young people into extremist networks. The sensitisation formed part of activities under the third quarter of the Atlantic Corridor Project, which seeks to prevent and respond to violent extremism in communities along the Atlantic Corridor, with funding support from the Governments of Denmark and Norway through the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). The programme followed the training of the Local Peace Committee (LPC) established in Binaba to help the community identify, prevent and respond to emerging threats to peace and security. Mr Damien Asobayire, the Upper East Regional Executive Secretary of the NPC, said the sensitisation was important because community members needed the knowledge and skills, to identify suspicious online narratives and report them through established community structures. He said violent extremist groups and their sympathisers increasingly used social media and other digital platforms to spread misleading information, hate speech and narratives capable of exploiting the frustrations and vulnerabilities of young people. “These are some of the things that community members need to know so that they can help prevent violent extremist activities in the community,” he said. Mr Asobayire urged residents to assist the LPCs by being monitors and share information on suspicious activities with the appropriate security authorities to enable early intervention. Mr David Atualing Angaamba, the Principal Programme Manager at the NPC, said although Ghana had not suffered a major violent extremist attack, several young people had been radicalised and recruited into extremist groups in the sub-region, with some eventually losing their lives. He therefore, urged the youth to be vigilant and critically assess information they received online, particularly attractive offers of employment, travel opportunities and financial rewards. Ms Fidelia Abariga, a participant said the sensitisation had made her more cautious about people who approached young persons with seemingly attractive opportunities. She recounted an experience in which some individuals allegedly came to the community offering young women opportunities to travel to Saudi Arabia for employment. “Some of them agreed and went there. As of now, we don’t know where they are. We can’t find them. They can’t call us, and we can’t also call them. We don’t even know whether they are alive or not,” she said. Ms Vida Amefo, another participant, said the programme had broadened her understanding of both the positive and negative effects of social media. She said the discussions had particularly exposed how social media could be exploited to spread misinformation, create fear, lure people with fake employment opportunities and facilitate the recruitment of vulnerable individuals. Ms Amefo pledged to share the knowledge gained with her family, church and other community members to promote vigilance and reduce their vulnerability to online manipulation. Reverend Issaka Ayande, a Pastor of the Assemblies of God Church, commended the NPC for organising the sensitisation and urged residents to take the lessons seriously. He said continuous community education was necessary to strengthen vigilance, promote responsible use of social media and prevent individuals, particularly the youth, from falling prey to extremist propaganda and fraudulent schemes.

items.title: IMCC seeks stronger decentralisation for local development‎
items.description: Dr Gameli Hoedoafia, Executive Secretary of the Inter-Ministerial Coordinating Committee on Decentralisation (IMCC), has called for a fundamental reset of Ghana’s decentralisation system to improve public service delivery and accelerate local development.‎ ‎He said the next phase of decentralisation must move beyond the establishment of institutions and transfer of functions to focus on the quality of services delivered, responsiveness of local institutions and tangible development outcomes for citizens.‎ ‎Dr Hoedoafia made the call on Monday at the opening of a two-day National Dialogue on Decentralisation and Responsive Governance in Accra, organised by the IMCC to deliberate on the future of decentralisation and promote responsive local governance.‎ ‎The dialogue, held on the theme: “Resetting Democratic Decentralisation for Accountable Public Service Delivery and Accelerated Local Development,” brought together regional ministers, Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs), traditional leaders, local government experts, development partners, civil society organisations and other stakeholders.‎ ‎It also coincided with the commemoration of African Decentralisation and Local Development Day (ADD), observed annually on August 10.‎ ‎Dr Hoedoafia said Ghana had made significant progress since the decentralisation process began more than three decades ago, but could not afford to become complacent, adding that existing local governance structures needed to be strengthened to deliver better outcomes.‎ ‎“Policy approval is not our finish line. It is our starting point. The real test now lies in coordination, effective implementation and delivery,” he said.‎ ‎Dr Hoedoafia said Cabinet’s approval of the National Decentralisation Policy and Strategic Framework (NDPS) 2026-2030 presented an opportunity to translate policy commitments into measurable improvements in the lives of citizens.‎ ‎He cautioned against allowing the framework to become another policy document without effective implementation, stressing the need for a coordinated, whole-of-government approach to decentralisation.‎ Dr Hoedoafia said the ultimate measure of decentralisation should be tangible improvements in communities, including roads, markets, health facilities, water systems, classrooms and other local infrastructure.‎ ‎He said the national dialogue would serve as an annual platform for reflection, accountability, partnership and action, bringing together government, local authorities, traditional leaders, development partners, civil society, academia, the private sector and citizens.‎ ‎Dr Hoedoafia urged stakeholders to renew their commitment to a local governance system that was democratic, accountable, adequately empowered and responsive to citizens’ needs.‎ ‎He said Ghana’s participation in the ADD provided an opportunity to reaffirm the country’s commitment to bringing governance closer to the people and ensuring that development reflected local priorities.‎ ‎Mr Ahmed Ibrahim, Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, said stronger financial support for Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs) was necessary to enable them to effectively deliver development to local communities.‎ ‎He said strengthening the capacity and financing of the MMDAs was critical to improving sanitation and building resilient communities.‎ ‎Mr Ibrahim said sanitation could not be addressed through policy alone, stressing the need for adequate resources, stronger inter-ministerial coordination, accountability and effective project execution at the local level.‎ ‎“Without adequate financial resources, we cannot build the capacity of our assemblies or deliver the sanitation and other essential services our communities need.‎ ‎“The MMDAs must have the fiscal space to invest in sanitation, water and other critical services, rather than merely administering scarcity,” he said.‎ ‎Mr Ibrahim said the Ministry had issued fee-fixing guidelines for 2026-2030 to establish transparent standards for fees, levies and charges.‎ ‎He said guidelines for the utilisation of the District Assemblies Common Fund (DACF) were also intended to provide assemblies with greater fiscal space to provide essential services.‎ ‎Mr Ibrahim called for stronger collaboration among the Ministry of Finance, MMDAs, development partners, civil society and other stakeholders to mobilise adequate resources for sanitation, drainage and flood mitigation.‎ ‎He also urged assemblies to strengthen revenue mobilisation, technical capacity, monitoring and accountability, stressing that policy frameworks alone could not deliver results without adequate financing.‎ ‎The Minister assured that the Government remained committed to providing the policy and fiscal frameworks needed to empower local authorities, but said sustained progress would depend on coordinated action, accountability and adequate resources.‎ ‎Madam Magdalene Wust, Deputy Head of Cooperation at the Embassy of Switzerland in Ghana, speaking on behalf of development partners, commended the Government for its continued commitment to decentralisation and the approval of the National Decentralisation Policy and Strategic Framework 2026-2030.‎ ‎She said the framework provided a critical basis for advancing decentralised governance, but called for stronger oversight, accountability, citizen participation and financial autonomy at the district level.‎ ‎Madam Wust stressed that national institutions must strengthen monitoring and supervision to ensure that subnational governments effectively delivered on their mandates.‎ ‎She assured that development partners remained committed to supporting Ghana’s decentralisation agenda through stronger coordination and strategic partnerships.‎

items.title: SHC seeks report over ‘delay’ in Mustafa Amir murder trial
items.description: KARACHI: The Sindh High Court (SHC) on Monday sought a report from an anti-terrorism court (ATC) on an application filed against a delay in the trial of the Mustafa Amir murder case. A two-judge regular bench of the SHC headed by Justice Muhammad Iqbal Kalhoro also said that the report must carry details about the progress made so far in the case at the trial court. The prime accused Armaghan, along with his accomplice Sheraz, has been facing trial for allegedly abducting and killing 23-year-old Mustafa Amir at the house of the main accused in the Defence Housing Authority in January last year as well as setting the body along with his car ablaze in the Hub area. Complainant Wajeeha Amir, mother of the victim, through her lawyer, filed a criminal miscellaneous application before the SHC against a delay in conclusion of the trial. The counsel argued that the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997, provides for an expeditious trial, but despite the passage of over one-and-a-half years, there was hardly any progress in the case. The lawyer also asserted that the accused side has consistently been using various tactics at the trial court to cause an inordinate delay in the proceedings. The applicant sought directives for the trial court to proceed with the matter expeditiously. After an initial hearing, the bench sought details and a progress report on the case from the ATC at the next date, to be fixed later by the office of the court. In February, the ATC had indicated both the accused persons and directed the prosecution witnesses to record their statements after the accused pleaded not guilty and opted to contest the case. Published in Dawn, August 11th, 2026

items.title: La course à l’IA a un problème structurel
items.description: Dans un document de travail publié en juillet 2026, l'économiste de la Banque des règlements internationaux, Phurichai Rungcharoenkitkul, modélise la construction des infrastructures d'intelligence artificielle comme une course, un « contest » au sens de la théorie économique, dans laquelle quelques positions dominantes capturent l'essentiel des gains The AI Investment Race », BIS Working Papers , n° 1367, Banque des règlements internationaux, juillet 2026.'> 1 . Sa thèse centrale est que la course à l'IA « engendre une fragilité qui la mine elle-même ». Le graphique ci-dessous, extrait du rapport, présente l'une des deux facettes du phénomène : son ampleur historique. Rapportée à son niveau le plus bas d'avant « le boom », la dépense d'investissement dans l'IA est sur le point de dépasser tous les grands épisodes de boom technologique en seulement trois ans. La courbe de l'IA monte plus vite et plus haut que celle de la canalmania américaine des années 1830, de la railway mania britannique des années 1840, des Années folles ou de la bulle Internet de la fin des années 1990. Les dépenses des grands hyperscalers devraient dépasser 700 milliards de dollars pour l'année 2026 seulement, et les projections du secteur tablent sur 3 000 à 4 000 milliards pour les prochaines années. Tous les épisodes historiques cités se sont achevés par des corrections brutales. La pente actuelle n'est pas un gage de solidité, mais le signe d'une sur-construction quantifiée, qui rend les booms les plus susceptibles de se retourner. Ce phénomène est provoqué par une caractéristique typique de la course. La victoire est telle que « le vainqueur remporte presque tout » : chaque acteur investit donc massivement pour distancer ses rivaux, sans tenir compte de l'impact de sa course sur les autres. Selon le modèle calibré, le résultat est un sur-investissement d'environ 1,5 fois le niveau socialement optimal, et jusqu'à trois fois là où la demande d'IA est moins élastique. Cette dynamique a toutefois un seuil critique. Une fois que la construction atteint un certain seuil, que l'auteur situe autour de 3 000 milliards de dollars, le surplus économique net (production totale moins coût du capital) deviendrait négatif. Les projections situées entre 3 000 et 4 000 milliards de dollars placeraient donc le secteur « dans la zone des risques baissiers significatifs », écrit-il. Le capital ainsi accumulé est spécialisé. En cas de retournement, il devrait être liquidé simultanément sur un marché peu liquide, ce qui réduirait d'autant le taux de récupération, surtout compte tenu de l'endettement du secteur. L’analyse se concentre également sur un deuxième problème central, celui du financement circulaire de l’IA. Le phénomène est le suivant : un acteur prend une participation au capital d'un laboratoire d'IA en échange de l'engagement de ce dernier à lui acheter de la puissance de calcul future. La demande est ainsi « fabriquée » par ceux qui financent l'offre. Le réseau relie ainsi les hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Oracle et Meta), les fabricants de puces (Nvidia et AMD), les laboratoires (OpenAI, Anthropic et xAI) et le principal néocloud (CoreWeave). L'ordre de grandeur est impressionnant : environ 46 milliards de dollars de participations ont été effectivement déboursés, mais les engagements d'achat pluriannuels s'élèvent à 879 milliards. Ces participations croisées ne font que concentrer le risque. L'auteur réume : « Le montage financier qui a alimenté la croissance est également celui qui transmet la faillite ». En abandonnant l'hypothèse d'acteurs isolés pour modéliser le réseau réel, le rapport met ainsi en lumière une nouvelle vulnérabilité : la défaillance d'un seul laboratoire pourrait, en affectant le bilan de l'hyperscaler qui le finance, inciter ce dernier à se désengager d'un autre laboratoire, propageant ainsi la crise. Ce risque s'aggraverait à mesure que la course se poursuit. Selon la simulation, la première cascade se situerait à une échelle d'investissement de 1,6 fois le niveau optimal, la seconde à 2,3 — et la trajectoire annoncée de 3 000 à 4 000 milliards projetterait le secteur dans cette zone de contagion (entre 2,1 et 2,9). Ainsi, plus le financement passe par plusieurs laboratoires reliés entre eux par quelques nœuds « pivots », plus une défaillance locale peut devenir systémique. L'auteur note aussi que la demande potentielle en IA est « vaste » et pourrait justifier une expansion considérable de la puissance de calcul. Toutefois, il souligne que la logique de course incite à sur-construire. L’article La course à l'IA a un problème structurel est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Veep urges stakeholders to support decentralisation policy implementation‎
items.description: Vice President Professor Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang has urged stakeholders to support implementation of Ghana’s decentralisation framework.‎ ‎She said the National Decentralisation Policy and Strategic Framework (NDPS) 2026-2030 required collective commitment to translate decentralisation reforms into improved services and tangible development outcomes.‎ ‎Prof. Opoku-Agyemang made the call in Accra on Monday when she opened the Second National Dialogue on Decentralisation and Responsive Governance, organised by the Inter-Ministerial Coordinating Committee on Decentralisation (IMCC).‎ ‎The dialogue brought together regional ministers, Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs), traditional leaders, local government experts, development partners, civil society organisations and other stakeholders.‎ ‎It also coincided with the commemoration of the African Decentralisation and Local Development Day, observed annually on August 10.‎ ‎The Vice President said stakeholder support could take the form of technical assistance, capacity development, financing, advocacy, innovation and active participation.‎ ‎“Government action alone will not be enough,” she said, stressing the need for collective efforts to strengthen local governance and ensure that decentralisation delivered meaningful results to communities.‎ ‎The NDPS 2026-2030, approved by Government, seeks to deepen the transfer of functions and responsibilities to the local level, strengthen local governance institutions, improve public service delivery and accelerate development.‎ ‎It also seeks to enhance citizen participation and accountability while strengthening collaboration between central and local governments and other stakeholders.‎ ‎Prof. Opoku-Agyemang said the framework was not merely a policy document but a roadmap for building a governance system in which local institutions had the confidence, capacity and resources to respond effectively to local needs.‎ ‎She said Government’s commitment to decentralisation was further reinforced by its position paper on constitutional review recommendations, which sought to strengthen local governance, enhance accountability and reinforce the democratic legitimacy of local governments.‎ ‎Prof. Opoku-Agyemang said Government had re-energised the IMCC and ncreased the proportion of the District Assemblies Common Fund transferred directly to MMDAs.‎ ‎It was also advancing policy and legislative work to deepen functional devolution in education, health and roads.‎ ‎On sanitation, Prof. Opoku-Agyemang said recent flooding had exposed weaknesses in waste management, sanitation practices and enforcement of environmental standards.‎ ‎She said the proposed District Environment, Health and Sanitation Department under the NDPS would restore operational responsibility for environmental health and sanitation to MMDAs.‎ ‎The Vice President said sanitation performance had also become a key performance indicator for MMDCEs, adding: “Cleanliness must become a daily discipline.”‎ ‎She urged stakeholders to measure decentralisation by its impact on citizens, rather than only by policies, structures and functions transferred.‎ ‎“Our aim is a Ghana where local institutions have the confidence, the capacity and the resources to respond to local needs and where communities are active partners in shaping development,” she said.‎ ‎Mr Ahmed Ibrahim, Minister for Local Government, Decentralisation and Religious Affairs, called for stronger financial support for MMDAs to enable them to effectively bring development to local communities.‎ ‎He said strengthening the capacity and financing of MMDAs was critical to improving sanitation and building resilient communities.‎ ‎Mr Ibrahim said sanitation could not be addressed through policy alone, stressing the need for adequate resources, stronger inter-ministerial coordination, accountability and effective project execution at the local level.‎ ‎“Without adequate financial resources, we cannot build the capacity of our assemblies or deliver the sanitation and other essential services our communities need.‎ ‎“The MMDAs must have the fiscal space to invest in sanitation, water and other critical services, rather than merely administering scarcity,” he said.‎ ‎Mr Gameli Hoedoafia, Executive Secretary of the IMCC, said the new phase of decentralisation must focus on democratic participation, accountable public service delivery and accelerated local development.‎ ‎He urged stronger coordination, effective implementation and measurable delivery to ensure that the framework did not remain merely a policy document.‎ ‎Mr Hoedoafia also asked stakeholders to measure success by the quality of services delivered and tangible improvements in communities, rather than only by functions transferred or institutions established.‎ ‎“Democratic participation, accountable public service delivery and accelerated local development must define this new phase of decentralisation.‎ ‎“We must move from measuring decentralisation by the functions transferred and institutions established to measuring it by the quality of services delivered, the responsiveness of local institutions and the development outcomes experienced by citizens across the country,” he said.‎

items.title: The tipping point of change
items.description: DISCUSSIONS are happening about how so many of the young protesters that rocked the Modi government recently came from families that have been faithfully voting for the right-wing prime minister. A crucial fact that seems to elude the discussants is that liberal or communist or fascist ideologues are not hatched in hatcheries. Unlike Narendra Modi, they are not ‘non-biological’ beings that gatecrash our earthly world. To begin with, it would be useful to bear in mind that the jailed left-wing student leader Umar Khalid had transcended to secular left politics from circumstances in which his father was a member of a major Muslim revivalist body. Likewise, Neha Bora, president of the pro-communist All-India Students’ Association who fasted for 23 days at the protest, tells you sans demur that she broke away from a family tradition of voting for the Muslim-baiting BJP. The flow can be in the opposite direction too. Howard Fast, as the despairing chief of the US Communist Party, famed for writing the story of Spartacus, the slave rebel of Rome, became a Buddhist seeker after abandoning Marxism. Numerous such examples abound in the Indian intellectual pantheon of progressivism and regression, which we can discuss. A scene is vivid from my childhood in which the migration to progressive politics would seem facile despite the good intentions. It was a balmy morning in Mustafabad, a village of erstwhile Shia taluqdars in the heart of Uttar Pradesh. Some young men and women in the joint family had recently got the first university degrees. Marxism was in the air in university campuses in the 1960s. That morning the tea was of just the right temperature, its bouquet flavourful. Three bespectacled young men from among the learned ones were steeped in a discussion that straddled Marx, Nehru, Josh and Neruda. The men were wrapped in embroidered woollen shawls over spotless white muslin kurta-pajama attires when the mehtrani, the woman carrying human refuse in an open reed basket, walked past. Other than putting the handkerchiefs on their faces briefly, the men remained unabashedly unperturbed in their intellectual chatter. A follower of Dalit politics would have reacted differently to the brutal absurdness of the frame. Indian communists added B.R. Ambedkar and the sickening caste angle to their class analysis grudgingly, only recently harnessing it to the dialectical quiver. These early activists had the theory but not the praxis, which would take years to arrive, or perhaps not. It’s not clear that most of the youth who defied the fierce police assault the other day had, in fact, crossed the tipping point from their social reality. Thus, it’s not even clear that most of the youth who defied the fierce police assault the other day to scare the hell out of a stubborn authoritarian government had, in fact, crossed the tipping point from their social reality. A Buddhist would call the migration nirvana — the blowing out of greed, hatred and ignorance. Collectively, the youth displayed a healthy mix of all three characteristics. When and if they reassemble it could be a different variety of mix. Arvind Kejriwal had held out a similar promise when his Aam Aadmi Party stop­ped the Hindutva juggernaut in Delhi in 2015. The ‘Modi wave’ had taken care of Maharashtra and Haryana state polls in quick succession. Kejriwal stopped the BJP chariot in Delhi. Then something equally important occurred. He rejected the offer of support from the Shahi Imam of Jama Masjid, and people were emboldened to believe that the time had come to separate religion from politics as the constitution ordains. Then in a crude display of regressive religiosity, he started holding election campaigns from Hindu temples and wooed senior voters with offers of free Hindu pilgrimages. One doesn’t have to agree with T.S. Eliot who says: “Youth is cruel and has no remorse. And smiles at situations it cannot see.” But youth is a handy demographic factor with an uncertain political trajectory. Not long ago, taking on the same Modi establishment, a courageous woman had single-handedly instigated the downfall of Modi’s minister accused of sexual transgressions. But the same charges failed to secure the conviction of a BJP muscleman. However, there again is the unforgettable instance of determined and seasoned farmers who forced the cancellation of Modi’s prized anti-farm laws. It is heartening to remember, therefore, that the Cockroach leaders have committed themselves to deter violations of citizen’s voting rights by a wayward election commission. The youth are committed to take on the hopelessly compromised corporate media that misreported the protests. Keeping company in the progressive transition of Khalid and Bora are some very eminent intellectuals of the subcontinent. Faiz Ahmed Faiz’s path from traditional Islamic education to becoming one of South Asia’s most iconic Marxist intellectuals highlights a fascinating evolution. Majro­­oh Sultanpuri was destined to become a hakim, for which he had acquired a degree. Then he turned towards left politics and endured isolation and even jail for his beliefs. I recently saw lovely pictures of Faiz’s daughters on a holiday in Sri Lanka. Had DPT been around, they would have in all likelihood been in India for he had the magic of fixing visas for all manner of progressive Pakis­tanis. Devi Prasad Tripathi came to JNU from the RSS stable. He became a staunch member of the Communist Party of India-Marxist and won the election as student union president when he was arrested and jailed during the emergency. Many political stalwarts left the RSS to become leftists and are leading critics of the Modi establishment. Kaifi Azmi became a progressive writer after early inspiration from the valour of Imam Husain. And, Iran has shown that a just battle can harness religious motifs to thwart a powerful aggressor. “ Dekhna Kaifi nishan-i-hurriyat lahraega/ Jab jahan ko azm-i-Sher-i-Karbala mil jayaega ” (‘Watch, O Kaifi, the banner of freedom shall flutter high/ Once the world finds the Lion of Karbala and joins his battle cry’). Kaifi’s pre-Marxist verses presaged the retreat of imperialism not far from the site of the students’ protest. And Iran’s left? They’re cohabiting with imperialism. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi. jawednaqvi@gmail.com Published in Dawn, August 11th, 2026

items.title: Equal citizens
items.description: AUG 11 occupies a special place in our history because it was on this day in 1947 that Quaid-i-Azam Mohammad Ali Jinnah set out what citizenship in the new state ought to mean. Addressing the Constituent Assembly, he spoke of a country in which people were free to go to their temples, mosques or other places of worship, and where religion, caste or creed would not determine their standing before the state. He insisted that citizens should enjoy equal rights, privileges and obligations, and that discrimination between communities had no place in the order Pakistan was attempting to build. These remarks formed part of a wider vision of government based on law, impartiality, protection of life and property, and the safeguarding of religious belief. It is fitting, then, that minority rights activists will gather outside Mazar-i-Quaid in Karachi today to recall that promise and demand that it be honoured. The Minority Rights March has put forward 11 demands, including stronger safeguards against forced conversions, protection from the misuse of blasphemy laws, greater political representation, removal of discriminatory material from textbooks, protection of minority properties and places of worship, and expanded access to education and employment. Organisers have also called for constitutional amendments allowing non-Muslim citizens to qualify for the offices of president and prime minister. Whether every demand commands consensus is a matter for democratic debate. But the principle from which they proceed — that citizenship should not be graded according to faith — should not be controversial in a republic that continues to invoke Jinnah as its founding authority. The delay in a written NOC for the march deserves attention. Peaceful assembly is a right, not a favour. The gap between Jinnah’s principle of equal citizenship and present realities cannot be ignored. It is especially troubling because these protections were articulated at the birth of Pakistan itself. Religious minorities continue to face mob violence, attacks on their places of worship, forced conversions and social and economic exclusion. Laws intended to protect religion have at times been weaponised through false accusations, with consequences extending far beyond the courtroom. Even where the state guarantees equality, social prejudice and institutional barriers make that guarantee fragile in practice. National Minority Rights Day must be more than a ceremonial observance. It should prompt the state to examine where law, policy and public culture continue to fall short of the standard articulated on Aug 11, 1947. Jinnah did not ask minorities to be grateful for protection; he described equal citizenship as a fundamental principle. Pakistan cannot honour that principle through speeches alone. It will honour it when every citizen, regardless of faith, can claim the same dignity, security and political belonging. Published in Dawn, August 11th, 2026

items.title: Bolgatanga Municipal Assembly invests DACF in schools, CHPS compounds
items.description: The Bolgatanga Municipal Assembly has invested portions of its District Assemblies Common Fund (DACF) in the construction and upgrading of basic education and healthcare infrastructure, to improve access to quality social services in deprived communities. The projects, which are at various stages of completion, included kindergarten (KG) blocks, a Junior High School (JHS) block, Community-based Health Planning and Services (CHPS) compounds and other ancillary facilities. Mr Roland Atanga Ayoo, the Bolgatanga Municipal Chief Executive (MCE), disclosed this when he led a team from the Assembly to inspect ongoing development projects across the Municipality. He said the projects formed part of the Assembly’s efforts to bridge infrastructure gaps, particularly in rural communities where residents had limited access to education and healthcare facilities. The MCE said the Assembly was constructing two KG blocks with urinals at Yorogo-Gabisi and Dorongo-Aperiga, while a modern three-unit classroom block at Kulgo-Aguusi was also nearing completion. The Kulgo-Aguusi facility comprised an Information and Communication Technology (ICT) room, library, staff common room, headmaster’s office, store, four-seater KVIP toilet and separate two-unit urinals for boys and girls. Mr Ayoo said the KG blocks at Gabisi and Aperiga as well as the Kulgo-Aguusi JHS projects, had been completed and would soon be handed over to the Ghana Education Service (GES) for use. He said the provision of educational infrastructure in rural communities would enable more children, particularly those at the kindergarten level, to access formal education closer to their homes. The MCE also said several CHPS compounds had been completed or were nearing completion and would soon be handed over to the Ghana Health Service (GHS). He said the investment in health infrastructure was particularly important because several communities in the Municipality were located far from the main town, making access to healthcare difficult for residents. “By providing such facilities, people will be able to access healthcare,” he said. Mr Ayoo said the Assembly was also undertaking renovation works and other development projects as part of efforts to improve living conditions and promote socio-economic development within the Municipality. He however, expressed concern about delays in the construction of the Sawaba CHPS compound, saying the Assembly’s engineer had issued a warning letter to the contractor and invited him to explain the reasons for the delay. He said the contractor had initially started the project ahead of the others but had subsequently fallen behind schedule. “I cannot tell for a fact what the problem is, but I have asked the engineer to call him and we will find out what is happening,” he said. The MCE urged residents to take ownership of the projects and protect public infrastructure to ensure that the investments served their intended purposes. He said the Assembly’s development interventions were intended to complement national efforts to improve education and healthcare delivery and promote development in the Municipality.

items.title: Cocoa Bill put ‘cart before horse’ – Frimpong Addo blasts post-passage farmer consultations
items.description: Former Deputy Minister for Agriculture and Cocoa Affairs, Yaw Frimpong Addo, has criticised the process leading to the passage of the new Cocoa Bill. The Manso Adubia MP says key stakeholders were not adequately consulted before the legislation was passed. According to him, the Minority is not opposed to every provision in the Bill but has identified specific areas it considers problematic for cocoa farmers. “It’s not everything in the bill that we, the minority, are saying is not good for the farmers. We have listed the key areas where we think are problematic, and that the president should not assent this bill until the until enough consultation is done,” he said. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Monday, Mr Frimpong Addo also insisted that the Minority’s input was necessary in the passage of such an important piece of legislation. He said the involvement of the parliamentary Agriculture Committee came too late in the process. “It came too late in the day when the referral was made that the Agric committee leadership was to join the finance committee and then the legal affairs committee to look at the bill,” he said. He questioned why a major stakeholder such as the Agriculture Committee was not involved from the beginning. “A major stakeholder like the Agriculture committee in Parliament. So when all this information was not coming, our leadership made sure that no nobody took part in the in the deliberations at all,” he said. Mr Frimpong Addo said the Minority’s decision not to participate was informed by what he described as its exclusion from the process from the outset. “Because in the first place they didn’t see the essence of including the minority in the deliberations from day one, and that for us was not too good for the bill to pass,” he said. He also raised concerns about the exclusion of cocoa hauliers from consultations on the Bill. According to him, the people who transport cocoa from producing areas to the ports are important stakeholders in the industry. “You know, we have hauliers also in the scheme of things when we talk about the cocoa industry, those who haul the cocoa from the hinterlands to the ports, and these people make those stakeholders, they were not consulted. They were not consulted,” he said. He, therefore, called for a thorough review of the legislation and wider consultations before it is assented to. “So we think that fundamentally there are problems. There are challenges with the Bill, and we need a thorough look at it,” he said. Mr Frimpong Addo’s strongest objection, however, was directed at consultations being held with farmer groups after Parliament had already passed the Bill. “From there, a lot of consultations will have to take place because what they have done is like putting the cart before the horse,” he said. He said reports that consultations were now being held with farmers’ groups were unacceptable. “It came to our notice that they are now going round having meetings with farmers’ groups and all that. After the bill has been passed, that is not normal. That’s not correct,” he said.

items.title: Topic of no importance
items.description: THE past couple of weeks have been packed with news and not just of the international kind. There were elections in Azad Kashmir , verbal duelling between the PPP and PML-N and an intense debate on a system that has collapsed. And in the midst of this came the matter of superior sounding administrative units versus local governments. What more could a journalist want? Yet more bad news it seems. For there was a relatively unimportant news item in the oft-ignored city pages of this paper, which announced a new underpass at the injunction of Margalla Road and Eighth Avenue. It seems as if someone, somewhere in the hallways of CDA has decided the short wait at the crossing is a wait too long. And Dubai-like, the rich residents of Islamabad should also not have to wait at all, for modernity means zooming around wide roads. So a new underpass the city shall have — at a junction where the avenue is called Faisal Avenue, for it leads up to the mosque, in the green lap of the Margallas. It is hard to keep count of the underpasses and flyovers CDA has inflicted upon this small city, especially in recent times. The new boss of the city, Mohsin Naqvi, is surely inspired by his boss, Shehbaz Sharif. As chief minister of Punjab, Naqvi was praised for his ‘Mohsin speed’, a term which paid homage to him and Shehbaz Sharif who too had been awarded a similar epithet. Both were praised for the speed at which they built projects. It’s hard to keep count of the underpasses and flyovers CDA has inflicted on Islamabad. In a country where visible brick-and-mortar projects pass for development, speed is seen as a virtue, rather than decision-making which is sustainable and helps improve people’s lot. And while Shehbaz junior now does illustrate the difference between building bridges and running a country, Naqvi has brought the speedy flair to Islamabad, where CDA has built flyovers in every nook and cranny of the city that can fit one. After all, if Shehbaz Sharif could take away university land to build roads, why can’t others build on existing roads? In so doing, the current government has contributed to turning a small green city into a grey shadow of Lahore. It is more unfortunate for the capital, for Islamabad has little of the old charm or history that Lahore can lay claim to. The greenery and hills are all the capital can offer but between its rapid expansion, numerous housing societies, and our planners’ obsession with Dubai-style traffic, Islamabad is losing its uniqueness. Over time, the construction is also becoming as durable as the governments in Islamabad. Each time, it rains, a newly built road reveals the poor standards of construction, so much so that media organisations are stopped from covering the quick wear and tear. This was seen when the roads in front of a known hotel needed quick repairs after rain, and when a fancy sculpture at a new roundabout couldn’t withstand a monsoon spell. But it was perhaps just a coincidence for had the construction standards been really poor, more attention would have been paid to another news story that got very little attention. Recently, a story appeared in a paper about audit objections to the new underpass built near the F-9 park in Islamabad. It reported that the audit highlighted faults in the design of the underpass. However, the little attention that was paid to the story shows it really wasn’t all that significant or newsworthy. My objections however are different. Dangerous turns in underpasses, which require cars to suddenly slow down, are hardly important in a city built for speed — half of Islamabad is now built to allow vehicles to zip around. However, why do those running this city want ugly bridges and underpasses near the F-9 park? For those who are unfamiliar with Islamabad, the F-9 park comprises an entire sector in the heart of the city and perhaps is comparable to Central Park in Manhattan, New York. Anywhere else in the world, such a large green space would be protected and so would the real estate around it. But not in Islamabad. Years ago, a part of it was given to an international franchise; despite a court order, the city found a way to let the corner be, and even give it legal cover. Now, two sides of the park boast flyovers that obstruct the view of the greenery. Imagine if someone suggested constructing bridges on Fifth Avenue next to Central Park. In Pakistan, we have no such concerns. Cars have a need to speed through signal-free corridors — and if it means ruining the roads and the serene views next to the city’s green spaces, so be it. And now Faisal Avenue is next. It is a wide road so named because it leads down to the Faisal Mosque, synonymous with Islamabad in some ways. The decision, it seems, has been made — and with little input from either the city’s residents or others. If some feel the idea is not a good one, there is little that can be done about it. And neither can the courts provide a recourse — for obvious reasons. It may seem like a frivolous issue to write about at a time when so much is happening in the country and the region, but there is a point to be made here. The local government or smaller provincial debate is not an abstract one about what theory says. And neither will it yield the results its proponents are boasting about if the representatives are not accountable to the people. And accountability, first and foremost, comes from genuine representation. If the residents of Islamabad had that, instead of bureaucrats and MNAs with controversial electoral wins, perhaps some of this construction could have been questioned. The writer is a journalist. Published in Dawn, August 11th, 2026

items.title: Colombia, bajo el estado de emergencia por el terremoto que causa más de 130 muertos
items.description: Colombia todavía cuenta sus muertos. El país amanecerá este martes bajo el estado de emergencia nacional, después de que un terremoto de magnitud 7,4 sacudió la víspera durante cuatro eternos minutos el oeste del país, y se sintió hasta Panamá y Ecuador. Los coletazos del temblor –el de mayor magnitud desde 1979– han dejado hasta el momento más de un centenar de muertos y más de 500 heridos, con decenas de edificios completamente colapsados. Al menos 132 personas han fallecido, de acuerdo con el más reciente balance de la Asociación Colombiana de Ciudades Capitales (Asocapitales). Las cifras todavía se consideran preliminares.
